title: Thoreau close
hookLine: our weeks at Walden end where he began: I went to the woods

cards: "I lived there two years and two months." That's how Thoreau sums up his stay at Walden, early in the book, almost in passing, adding that he's a sojourner in civilized life again. A short stay, then back to town.

This path's own stay with him has been a few weeks of mornings: a cabin, a pond, a jail, a mountain, a shore, a journal, a friend's honest tribute. Today the cabin door closes with the sentence that opened it.

teach.b: From Walden's second chapter, a line this path first met back in year one: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived."
First, deliberately: not by accident, not by habit, not because everyone else was doing it. On purpose.

Second, the essential facts. To front them means to face them head-on. Not the news, not the gossip, not the shopping, but what is actually basic: food, shelter, work, the seasons, other people, death.
Third, learn what it had to teach.
He went as a student, not a conqueror; the woods were the teacher. Every chapter was a lesson he took down: the pond's depth, the ant war, the thawing bank, contact on the mountain.

Fourth, he left: "I left the woods for as good a reason as I went there." He doesn't say the experiment failed; he had other lives to live. That matters, because this path isn't asking anyone to move to a cabin.
The woods weren't the point. Living deliberately was. You can go to the woods for an hour on a Saturday, for ten minutes in a city park, or by stepping outside to look at the sky before bed.
Thoreau's books are an open door, not a fence. And tomorrow a new road opens: what happens when people who meditate sit down with people who measure the mind.

how: Some readers who finish Walden take from it a habit of going outdoors on purpose, for an hour or an afternoon, to live a little more deliberately rather than to move to a cabin.

games.why: Thoreau left, and said it was for as good a reason as he went there. he had other lives to live.

practice: Picture a place you could actually reach this week, a park, a path, a backyard, a quiet street with trees, and see yourself there for an hour with nowhere to be, no headphones, no goal.
Ask Thoreau's question quietly: what might it have to teach? Hold the picture a while.
